description: Two physicians working on the challenge Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions.
summary: Astronauts on long missions can develop blood clots in the jugular vein: in NASA data, 8 of 31 astronauts had a left jugular flow anomaly in flight. VTE Watch keeps NASA's July 2026 VTE Risk Score for Astronauts word for word, every point with its NASA rule and source, and builds a longitudinal monitoring and decision-support layer around it: an append-only record with provenance, separate ultrasound, lab, wearable and symptom timelines, explainable trend states, a symptom red-flag override that no low score can hide, a Flight Surgeon Console that sorts the whole crew by the agent's priority, a medication and landing check from NASA and FDA references, and a signed flight-surgeon packet. Every safety check runs onboard with no network, because at Mars the ground's reply can take 80 minutes. The concept is one constrained onboard surveillance agent that watches each astronaut's scans, symptoms and data quality over time and flags concerns, with their evidence, for the flight surgeon; this prototype is its rule-based first step (no AI model, no live feed, no live alert). It never diagnoses or treats: the flight surgeon decides. Synthetic data only; not a diagnosis, prediction or prescription.
details: SIMULATION, synthetic data only. VTE Watch organizes NASA-referenced venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk, scans, symptoms and medication checks over the mission for flight-surgeon review. The concept is one constrained surveillance agent that watches the record over time and flags concerns, with their evidence, for the flight surgeon; this prototype implements its rule-based first step with fixed, source-linked rules (no AI model, no live feed, no live alert). It does not detect, diagnose or predict clots. What it does. (1) Scores VTE risk with NASA's VTE Risk Score for Astronauts (NASA/SP-20260005258 REV1, July 2026), word for word, unchanged: every point shows NASA's rule, the input and the source; the band is shown as a reference, never a prescription. (2) Keeps an append-only record with provenance on every value and four separate timelines (duplex ultrasound, lab, wearable telemetry, symptoms). Only a duplex ultrasound scan can feed NASA's <10 cm/s stasis row or count as a scheduled scan; a wearable or an L+14 D-dimer never can, and nothing is filled in between scans; a chart plots each exam's left IJV velocity against NASA's 10 cm/s duplex criterion. (3) Gives an explainable state (DATA_INSUFFICIENT, RED_FLAG_OVERRIDE, DETERIORATING, WATCH, STABLE), never a competing score; STABLE is impossible above NASA's lowest bands. (4) A daily symptom report, signed by the team physicians: a new change in vision, hearing, pupils, face, grip, speech or confusion tells the astronaut to start the onboard emergency procedure now, whatever the score. (5) A Venous Flow Response Assessment log that needs a flight-surgeon order and exclusion checks and never claims lower risk. (6) A medication and landing check: NASA's apixaban references, the landing hold where NASA's two documents differ (24 h vs 48 h; the signed plan must choose), FDA-label interaction and bleeding flags, a bleeding-management inventory. It never starts, stops or doses anything. (7) A Flight-Surgeon Packet (JSON and one-page print): incomplete, stale or conflicting data mark it INCOMPLETE, never decision-ready. How it works. A static web app; all logic runs in the browser, offline. A Flight Surgeon Console (console.html) lists every synthetic crew member sorted by the agent's state, with the evidence for each. NASA's score is identical to the earlier Python-tested version on all cases. 12 synthetic crew cases (one per band and rule edge, a red-flag demo and a longitudinal demo) all match totals worked out by hand first. 163 automated tests. Three review rounds by an independent code reviewer and a clinical-safety reviewer that checked every quote against the NASA PDFs and the FDA label. Why it matters. NASA's new score is a table in a PDF, and in-flight evidence comes in sparse pieces. This keeps the score honest, the history visible, symptoms impossible to hide behind a low score, and clinical authority with the flight surgeon even when Earth is 40 minutes away. Limits. Synthetic data only. The team's trend rules are proposals, not validated; we measured no diagnostic or predictive performance. NASA notes D-dimer isn't routinely tested in flight. Validation would need individual-level in-flight jugular ultrasound with clinical outcomes. Tools and AI use. Plain HTML/CSS/JS, Python for the reference tests, Node's test runner, GitHub Pages. A separate on-demand script collects PubMed and NASA OSDR metadata into a cited review queue for the team; it is not part of the app. The idea and the v3.1 architecture are the team's. A teammate used ChatGPT (OpenAI) to explore features; the team's v3.1 and v3.2 implementation specifications were drafted with ChatGPT (OpenAI) from the team's chosen design and checked by the team (one v3.2 rule, "≥60%" for D-dimer, was not adopted because NASA's table says ">60%"); Claude Code (Anthropic) helped check sources, write and test code, and edit text; GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Argon reviewed earlier plans. Every code and data file is marked "AI-assisted". No AI-generated images or video. The 30-second demo film uses an AI voiceover and an AI music track, both made with ElevenLabs and labelled on screen; its visuals are real app screenshots of synthetic cases, drawn shapes and our own diagram, assembled with HyperFrames.
dataRefs: NASA/SP-20260005258 REV1: NASA Risk of Venous Thromboembolism in Spaceflight, Outcomes of Working Group Meeting, April 2026 (July 2026): VTE Risk Score for Astronauts, bands, stasis and D-dimer criteria, 8-of-31 IJV flow finding
OCHMO-MTB-007, Venous Thrombosis in Spaceflight: jugular ultrasound schedule
OCHMO-TB-007 Rev A, Mission Duration: communication latency and evacuation by destination
NTRS 20250002759, IMM vs IMPACT, Artemis II (AsMA 2025): lunar communication latency 5-14 s
NASA/SP-20260009389, DCS, VTE and PFO working group, August 2026 (context only, no rule): pre-EVA aspirin, aspirin with prophylactic apixaban, pain medicines that may mask DCS

NASA Open Science Data Repository, Inspiration4 studies OSD-575 and OSD-569: group summaries of fibrinogen, PF4 and platelet count, labelled context only, not used in scoring. Data are courtesy of the NASA Open Science Data Repository
projectRefs: ELIQUIS (apixaban) US prescribing information (FDA label, effective 17 Aug 2026, DailyMed), for drug-interaction and bleeding-risk flags only. No partner-agency data used; all crew data synthetic.
